items.to: Georgetown University (Center for Security and Emerging Technology, CSET)
items.capacity: launch funder of CSET; CSET's main funder as of Aug 2021
items.fact: Georgetown's 28 Feb 2019 announcement says a $55 million grant funded by the Open Philanthropy Project creates CSET. CSET's 25 Aug 2021 release says Open Philanthropy, its main funder, increased the grant by $42 million, bringing total funding above $100 million for 2019 to 2025.
items.quote: Funded by the Open Philanthropy Project, it will deliver nonpartisan analysis and advice
items.missing: Open Philanthropy's own grant record: the grant URL returned an unrelated Coefficient Giving page, not read. Tranche schedule. The Hewlett Foundation and Public Interest Technology University Network are named in CSET's 2021 release with no amounts.
items.notes: CSET 2021 release (https://cset.georgetown.edu/article/new-grant-agreement-boosts-cset-funding-to-more-than-100-million-over-five-years/, read) says: Open Philanthropy, CSET’s main funder, has just completed agreements with university officials to increase its grant by $42 million. A search summary also cites an $8M general-support grant to CSET; not read, unverified.

items.capacity: initial funder of the Horizon fellowship
items.fact: POLITICO, reported 13 Oct 2023 (read via Yahoo News), says Open Philanthropy set aside nearly $3 million in 2022 to pay for the initial cohort of Horizon fellows. The Chronicle of Philanthropy (30 Nov 2023, read) calls Open Philanthropy Horizon's initial funder.
items.publisher: POLITICO (Brendan Bordelon), syndicated on Yahoo News
items.quote: Open Philanthropy set aside nearly $3 million to pay for what ultimately became
items.missing: Open Philanthropy's own record of the Horizon grant. Horizon's current share of funding from Open Philanthropy (not disclosed in the Chronicle interview, per search summary). Total spending on fellows (declined by Open Philanthropy, per search summary).
items.notes: Chronicle of Philanthropy (https://www.philanthropy.com/article/can-a-nonprofit-help-lawmakers-understand-a-i, read) says Horizon’s initial funder, Open Philanthropy, was also an early backer of OpenAI, and that Open Philanthropy committed $30 million to OpenAI in 2017. That is an OpenAI tie, not an Anthropic one. Horizon’s co-founder and executive director Remco Zwetsloot is named in that article. Open Philanthropy's spokesperson response (Horizon began as consultants to Open Phil; no active role in screening, training or placing fellows) comes from a search summary of the Politico piece, not a verbatim read.

items.to: Department of Defense; Department of Homeland Security; State Department; House Science Committee; Senate Commerce Committee; offices of Sens. Heinrich, Rounds and Young
items.capacity: fellows whose salaries are funded by Open Philanthropy (current and former AI fellows)
items.fact: POLITICO (13 Oct 2023, read via Yahoo News) reports current and former Horizon AI fellows with Open Philanthropy-funded salaries working at DoD, DHS, the State Department, the House Science Committee and Senate Commerce, and names a Horizon fellow in each of Sens. Heinrich, Rounds and Young's offices. The Chronicle (30 Nov 2023, read) says placements are one or two years in Senate offices, congressional committees and federal departments, and at think tanks such as RAND and Brookings.
items.publisher: POLITICO (Brendan Bordelon), syndicated on Yahoo News; Chronicle of Philanthropy
items.quote: Current and former Horizon AI fellows with salaries funded by Open Philanthropy
items.missing: No Horizon placement at OSTP or the National Security Council was found in any source read, so those two bodies are not_found. Placement counts: the Washington Examiner Horizon piece (6 Nov 2025) reportedly gives 9 fellows in Republican-held and 6 in Democratic-held congressional offices, but the article body is paywalled and this comes from a search summary, so unverified. Horizon's own roster not read.
items.notes: Other Horizon counts, all from search summaries of different dates and not read: 50+ fellows (Founders Pledge evaluation); over 150 professionals into AI and biotech policy since 2022 (LongtermWiki summary of Horizon's 2025 review). TechCongress is a separate programme; see T9.12. Searches for 2021 to 2024 OSTP or NSC placements returned nothing specific.

items.capacity: hired by Matheny, then in senior Biden White House roles, under the Intergovernmental Personnel Act to help craft AI policy; Buchanan was then a top CSET staffer
items.fact: Washington Examiner's exclusive (17 Apr 2026, Robert Schmad, read) says FOIA documents show Matheny, who served in senior Biden White House roles from March 2021 to June 2022, hired Buchanan under the Intergovernmental Personnel Act. The article says the advisor and the staff they hired had ties to a nonprofit funded by a major investor in Anthropic; the visible text does not name that nonprofit or funder.
items.quote: hired Benjamin Buchanan, then a top staffer at CSET, using the Intergovernmental Personnel Act
items.missing: The article is paywalled after the lede, so the documents, the hire date and any other named officials in the body are not visible. A search snippet (not seen on the page read) says Sen. Ted Cruz objected to IPA hiring in letters to federal agencies and Buchanan defended it; unverified.
items.notes: Named officials in the visible text: Jason Matheny (founding director of CSET) and Benjamin Buchanan. Page header headline reads 'Documents show how a tech-connected nonprofit shaped Biden-era AI policy' (HTML title tag reads 'Biden's AI policy'). The article credits its Anthropic-linked staff hires to the IPA route; it does not say the hires were funded by any programme. Semafor (30 May 2025) separately reports White House complaints about Anthropic hiring former Biden staff; see T9.8.

items.from: Open Philanthropy / Horizon Institute for Public Service
items.fact: No source read or found names Buchanan or Collins as a Horizon fellow, or as funded or placed directly by Open Philanthropy. Buchanan's documented placement is his IPA hire by Matheny (Examiner, T9.4). Collins's CSET profile (read) lists only a Research Fellow role at CSET and a later role as Principal for Research and Strategy at DeepMind. Open Philanthropy is CSET's main funder (CSET 2021 release, T9.1).
items.publisher: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (staff profile)
items.quote: Tantum Collins was a Research Fellow at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET),
items.missing: Horizon's fellow rosters (Horizon's own website not read). Open Philanthropy grant lists naming Buchanan or Collins personally. Collins's National Security Council post: a search summary of a book listing says it; the CSET profile does not mention the NSC.
items.notes: Search summary of the book's listing (not read): Buchanan was White House special adviser for AI, June 2023 to January 2025, and Collins was NSC director for technology and national security. Buchanan is described as a senior faculty fellow at CSET. CSET is funded by Open Philanthropy, which is the organisational link only; no individual funding is stated.

items.capacity: individual investor participating in Anthropic's Series A (Open Philanthropy is not named as an investor)
items.fact: Anthropic's 28 May 2021 announcement (read) says a $124 million Series A led by Jaan Tallinn included participation from Dustin Moskovitz. POLITICO (Oct 2023, read via Yahoo) quotes a Moskovitz statement on his Anthropic investment; the announcement does not name Open Philanthropy as an investor.
items.quote: The round included participation from James McClave, Dustin Moskovitz
items.missing: Moskovitz's investment amount (not disclosed in pages read). The complete investor list. Later rounds: Yahoo/Politico says Anthropic was in talks with Google and other investors about an additional $2 billion (Oct 2023), not verified further.
items.notes: Politico quotes Moskovitz: any monetary returns from his Anthropic investment 'will be entirely redirected back into ou...' (text truncated in the page read). A LongTermWiki entry (search summary) names Moskovitz and Tallinn as Series A co-leads; the Anthropic announcement names Tallinn as lead and Moskovitz as a participant, so the announcement is taken as authoritative.

items.capacity: member of the technical staff, trust and safety work (per Fortune's report of Anthropic's confirmation)
items.fact: Fortune (13 Feb 2025, read) reports that Karnofsky, a co-founder of Open Philanthropy's predecessor work and Daniela Amodei's husband, joined Anthropic 'last month' as a member of technical staff; a company spokesperson confirmed. Fortune spells the name Karnofksy in the article.
items.quote: joined Anthropic last month as a member of the startup’s
items.missing: Exact start date (inferred as January 2025 from 'last month'). The date he left Open Philanthropy leadership (search summary says he stepped back in 2023; not read on a page). Founding date of Open Philanthropy (sources disagree: 2014 or 2017, per search summaries).
items.notes: Search summaries (not read): he ran Open Philanthropy as CEO and co-CEO until 2023; a Harvard profile says he works on Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy. Fortune (read) describes his role as trust and safety, reporting to Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan. Open Philanthropy has since been renamed Coefficient Giving (Open Philanthropy's own site, read).

items.capacity: adviser to Anthropic on safety and other issues
items.fact: Semafor (30 May 2025, read) lists Ben Buchanan, another Biden official, as an adviser to Anthropic, and says he has been working for Anthropic on safety and other issues. Semafor also reports White House officials complained about Anthropic hiring former Biden staff, including Elizabeth Kelly and Tarun Chhabra.
items.quote: Ben Buchanan, another Biden official, is an adviser.
items.missing: Start date and terms of the advisory role. Anthropic's own disclosure. Buchanan's current status (search summary says Johns Hopkins SAIS, not read).
items.notes: Search summaries (not read): Buchanan was White House special adviser for AI from June 2023 to January 2025 (Law.com summary) and holds a senior faculty fellowship at CSET. The Daily Beast also describes him as an adviser to Anthropic (search result, not read).

items.to: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
items.capacity: funder of GovAI (general support and field-building grants)
items.fact: page not read: the Open Philanthropy GovAI organisation URL returned Coefficient Giving's homepage. An EA Forum wiki summary in search results says GovAI had received nearly $3 million from Open Philanthropy as of July 2022; a search summary also says Open Philanthropy's grants list includes a General Support grant (Feb 2025) of about $3 million. Both figures are unverified.
items.publisher: EA Forum wiki (search result); Open Philanthropy grant database (not read)
items.missing: The GovAI grant records on Open Philanthropy's site, read directly. GovAI's annual report (funder list), not read. Survival and Flourishing Fund (over $600k) and EA Funds (over $170k) are search-summary figures only. The GovAI relaunch post (search result) thanks Open Philanthropy, the Centre for Emerging Risk Research and EA Funds.
items.notes: The brief places Collins on GovAI's team page. A search summary says a governance.ai page lists him as a CIP affiliate and a 2023-2024 Harvard fellow in residence (not read).

items.from: Funders of the Collective Intelligence Project
items.capacity: funders (no named funder list in the page text read)
items.fact: The CIP funders page (read) says its work is made possible by philanthropic partners and that it accepts no funding from commercial partnerships or contractual relationships, but the extracted text names no funders. Search summaries name grants from the Survival and Flourishing Fund ($300k, Jan 2023; $500k, 2024), the Ford Foundation ($100k core support, grantee RadicalXChange), Omidyar Network (LongTermWiki) and Future of Life Institute ($150k). None of these was read on a source page.
items.quote: Our work is made possible through the support of committed philanthropic partners
items.missing: A named funder list from CIP (the list did not appear in the extracted text; try the CIP annual reports). The SFF, Ford and Omidyar grant records read directly. Open Philanthropy funding of CIP: none found.
items.notes: Search summaries only, unverified: the Ford Foundation listing is for RadicalXChange as grantee. Do not confuse CIP with Nesta's separate Collective Intelligence Grants programme (funded by Omidyar, Wellcome and Cloudera, per search result).

items.to: White House (Office of Science and Technology Policy; National Security Council)
items.capacity: deputy assistant to the president for technology and national security; OSTP deputy director for national security; NSC coordinator for technology and national security
items.fact: CSET reproduces a MeriTalk report (11 Mar 2021, read) that CSET's founding director Jason Matheny took three Biden White House roles: deputy assistant to the president, OSTP deputy director for national security, and NSC coordinator for technology and national security. The Washington Examiner (17 Apr 2026, read) gives his senior White House service as March 2021 to June 2022.
items.quote: Matheny will serve as deputy assistant to the president for technology and national security
items.missing: Where Matheny went after June 2022: a search summary (University of Maryland ARLIS profile, which returned 404 on read) says president and CEO of RAND; unverified. No other former CSET person in a Biden-era AI policy role was confirmed (Tess deBlanc-Knowles and Asad Ramzanali appeared in results with no CSET link; Dewey Murdick ran CSET with no Biden-era role found).
items.notes: Other former CSET people for item 7 are Buchanan and Collins, covered in T9.4 to T9.8 and T9.5. Collins's CSET bio (read): Research Fellow at CSET, then Principal for Research and Strategy at DeepMind.

items.capacity: fellowship placing technologists in congressional offices
items.fact: LongTermWiki's TechCongress entry (read) describes a fellowship placing technologists in congressional offices, with 123 fellows placed to date. That wiki says it has not been maintained since May 2026, so treat it as low reliability. The entry does not state a funder or a 2021 to 2024 breakdown.
items.quote: Fellowship program placing technologists in congressional offices. 123 fellows placed to date
items.missing: Primary TechCongress source (techcongress.io), not read. Funder. Any OSTP or NSC placement. The 2021 to 2024 breakdown.
items.notes: Listed as a comparable programme under item 2. Not searched further (search budget used).
